title: Redwood cost-econ discovery with Summit Capital
summary: Discovery focused on per-token economics and options between hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. Customer has strict budget targets for cost/unit and wants clear levers (batching, KV caching, quantization) and an initial benchmark pathway. They requested pricing workbook, security docs, and a short pilot to validate latency and cost under their workloads.
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
next_steps: Jordan to send hosted vs dedicated pricing spreadsheet and example cost model by 2026-03-06
Maya to schedule 2-hour benchmark slot with Summit infra team week of 2026-03-09
Summit to share representative request traces (1-2 days) and success criteria by 2026-03-08
Jordan to attach SOC2 / ISO docs and architecture note for private deployment
action_items: Jordan Price | Send pricing workbook (hosted + dedicated + private delta) | due 2026-03-06
Maya Chen | Prepare benchmark runbook & sample scripts (loadgen + KV cache toggles) | due 2026-03-09
Priya Nair | Share 48h sample request traces + target p50/p95 latency and monthly token volume estimate | due 2026-03-08
Tom Delgado | Confirm VPC connectivity window for on-prem pilot | due 2026-03-10
transcript: [00:00] Jordan Price (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we're about 45 minutes on the invite, so i'll keep the intro short. who do we have from Summit?

[00:07] Priya Nair (Summit): Hi Jordan, Priya here - head of ML. Tom and Alicia are with me. we're evaluating options to run our LLM features, mostly inference, and want to understand cost per unit and what tradeoffs we get with hosted vs reserved capacity or running private.
[00:18] Jordan Price: great. quick intros - I'm Jordan (AE), Maya's our SE focused on performance and cost, and Liam is solutions. Maya, do you want to jump in on approach?

[00:27] Maya Chen (Redwood SE): yeah hi, thanks. we usually approach cost-econ discovery by mapping your request profile (tokens in, tokens out, concurrency, seq lengths) to per-token unit cost across hosting modes. then we show levers: batching, KV cache/prefix cache, quantization model variants, and routing policies. we can run a small benchmark with your traces to get actual numbers.
[00:42] Alicia Romero (Summit, FinOps): quick Q - when you say per-token cost, is that just model compute or are there other line items we should expect?

[00:48] Jordan Price: good call. hosted per-token includes compute and infra overhead and our managed service fee. dedicated/reserved gives you lower per-token compute but has commitment charges and you might pay for idle capacity. private has license/platform fees plus infra you manage. we'll break that down in the workbook.

[01:04] Tom Delgado (Summit): our primary constraints are: monthly budget cap of $40k for inference, p95 latency under 400ms for chat flows, and data never leaving our VPC for certain endpoints. Is that feasible?

[01:16] Maya Chen: totally reasonable. for p95 < 400ms we usually look at model size, seq length, and whether prefix caching helps. with hosted we can pin capacity or route to dedicated to meet your SLOs. for VPC/private we have a Private offering that runs in your VPC or on-prem with a control plane there are network and KMS implications we'll cover.
[01:34] Priya Nair: i'd like to understand the math — like if we batch at 8 vs 32 and use a KV cache with 60% cache hit, what happens to cost and latency?

[01:42] Maya Chen: yes the short answer: batching increases throughput and lowers cost per token, but can add queueing latency for single-user interactive flows. KV cache reduces compute by avoiding autoregressively recomputing prefix. in practice, with a 60% hit rate we often see 30-50% per-token cost reduction for generation-heavy workloads. batching from 8->32 can drop per-token compute cost by another 20-40% depending on model and kernels.

[02:05] Jordan Price: it's important to map those levers to your traffic patterns. if you have lots of short chat messages, large batch sizes hurt latency. we can suggest mixed policies: small batches for p95 sensitive routes, larger batches for async jobs. also quantized model variants (8-bit) can save costs but occasionally change output quality we run evals against your prompts.
[02:25] Alicia Romero: any sample numbers you can share now, ballpark?

[02:28] Maya Chen: ballpark hosted small-medium model after discounts might be $0.0008 - $0.002 per request-token depending on seq length and concurrency, but that's a wide range. dedicated reserved capacity could bring raw compute down ~30-60% per-token at scale, but you have the monthly commit. private adds infra costs but gives control for compliance.
[02:47] Tom Delgado: can you explain how KV cache and prefix caching actually works? we heard about KV cache but not sure how it fits with streaming/chat memory?

[02:54] Maya Chen: sure the runtime stores key/value cache for previous tokens. if you send a request that shares a prefix with a cached segment, runtime reuses KV entries and only computes the suffix, so less compute. for chat, we often keep a windowed cache for the system + recent turns. streaming can still work; we reconstruct outputs using cached kv for early tokens and compute new ones on the tail.
[03:16] Priya Nair: any gotchas for LLMs with long context? we have some flows that sometimes go to 4k tokens.

[03:21] Maya Chen: beyond certain lengths the kernel selection and memory bandwidth matter. we profile models and select kernels that trade compute for memory; quantization also impacts memory. we'll include kernel/profile recommendations in the report.

[03:35] Jordan Price: also routing policies can help cost: route low-latency critical traffic to dedicated or higher-tier hardware, and batch lower-priority traffic to cheaper variants or to scheduled windows.
[03:44] Alicia Romero: about commitments if we go dedicated, what's a typical commit level? and how elastic is it?

[03:50] Maya Chen: commits vary by company size; commonly customers commit to a baseline of GPUs or throughput and get lower unit pricing. we support autoscaling with burst allowances; the billing model reconciles usage vs commit monthly. we'll show an example commit that meets your $40k budget target and compare with hosted pay-as-you-go.
[04:05] Tom Delgado: what about private deployment network setup, KMS, and audit logs how intrusive is that?

[04:11] Jordan Price: Private requires a control-plane connector and a small agent; for on-prem you can choose air-gapped deployment. we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key management and provide audit logs and RBAC. we'll attach our architecture note and SOC2/ISO docs. Maya can follow up with the security checklist.

[04:26] Maya Chen: yes i'll send the security checklist. one caveat: private typically has higher upfront and operating costs since you run infra, but it's the path for strict data residency and compliance.
[04:36] Priya Nair: back to numbers can we do a pilot for say two models and run a 48-hour replay of our traffic to see actual cost figures?

[04:44] Jordan Price: absolutely. typical pilot: you share traces or we run a lightweight agent in your environment to replay; Maya runs runs with caching on/off and quantized vs fp16 models. we produce a cost delta table and latency distributions.
[04:57] Priya Nair: perfect. Alicia from FinOps side we want a simple projection: if we hit 5M tokens/month, how much and which option keeps us under $40k?
[05:06] Alicia Romero: yes that's the core ask i don't want too many knobs but i want to see clear dollar impact for each lever.

[05:12] Maya Chen: understood. we'll build a model in the workbook that takes tokens/month, hit rates, batch sizes, and shows per-token cost and monthly spend across hosted/dedicated/private. we'll also show break-even commit levels for dedicated.
[05:25] Tom Delgado: what about downstream costs like network egress or storage for KV caches?

[05:29] Jordan Price: storage for KV cache is typically small but depends on your retention window. network egress is a customer cloud cost for private deployments; hosted includes outbound bandwidth in the price up to usual limits. we'll outline that separately.
[05:40] Priya Nair: any issues with PII in traces? we may need to scrub before sending sample data.

[05:44] Maya Chen: we recommend scrubbing and can accept hashed identifiers. for pilot runs you can sanitize traces; if you need a secure channel we can use our Data Transfer spec and SFTP or direct VPC peering for private runs.
[05:57] Jordan Price: quick note on evals and quality quantization can change outputs slightly; we'll run a small eval set so you can see whether quality regressions are acceptable for your use case.
[06:07] Alicia Romero: how often do customers re-tune batch sizes? is that operationally heavy?

[06:11] Maya Chen: we recommend starting with conservative batch sizes for latency-critical routes and larger batches for background jobs. Redwood Optimize can suggest batch and quantization profiles by workload; it's not heavy once you have metrics streaming into the console.

[06:23] Jordan Price: wanted to call out two artifacts we will share: 1) pricing workbook with cost model and commit examples, 2) benchmark runbook + scripts and security checklist. we'll link those in follow up.
[06:33] Tom Delgado: about model variants do you support autoswitching between fp16 and int8 if a route is behind?

[06:38] Maya Chen: yes we have model variants and smart routing. you can configure fallbacks: if capacity is constrained, route to a compatible lower-cost variant or to dedicated pools. that helps availability versus strict quality-invariant SLAs.
[06:52] Priya Nair: competitor question did you compare to Anthropic or OpenAI in your benchmarks?

[06:56] Jordan Price: we do comparative benchmarks when customers ask, and include estimates for API pricing parity. Anthropic/OpenAI numbers vary by model; we can include a short competitive note but primary focus will be your actual workload numbers.
[07:08] Alicia Romero: for decision timeline, we're aiming to choose a vendor by end of month so a pilot next week would be tight but ideal.
[07:15] Jordan Price: we can prioritize. Maya, can you run a 48h replay next week if they provide traces by Monday?
[07:21] Maya Chen: yes, if we get traces Monday we'll aim to run bench Wed-Thu and have results by Friday. need a 2-hour connectivity window for VPC or agent install.
[07:30] Tom Delgado: we'll aim to have sanitized traces by Monday. one more technical Q: what's your cold-start behavior for model shards do you spin up warm pools?

[07:36] Maya Chen: for hosted we maintain a warm pool for common allocations; dedicated can keep pinned instances. cold starts are minimized via warmup and continuous batching. we'll expose warmup and eviction config so you can tune cost vs cold-start latency.
[07:52] Priya Nair: good. Alicia is there anything else from FinOps?
[07:55] Alicia Romero: just that the workbook should surface sensitivity to cache hit rates i need to see best-case/worst-case monthly spend.
[07:59] Jordan Price: understood. we'll include a sensitivity table (cache hit 20/40/60/80%).
[08:06] Priya Nair: can you give an example row of the workbook now? like 5M tokens/month, 60% cache hit, batching 16 what would be rough monthly spend hosted?

[08:14] Maya Chen: rough ballpark assuming an effective per-token compute of $0.0009 with those levers, 5M tokens ~ $4.5k compute plus managed fees, call it ~$6k hosted. with dedicated that might be reduced to ~$3.5k if you're near steady-state and commit to baseline. these are illustrative; the pilot will give exacts.
[08:34] Tom Delgado: wow that's lower than i expected great. what's the typical delta for private?

[08:38] Jordan Price: private often has higher ops cost but gives compliance and predictable unit costs you control; the platform fee and infra may push first-month costs up but long-term depending on scale you can beat hosted or dedicated.

[08:49] Alicia Romero: ok let's capture deliverables Jordan you'll send workbook and SOC2 docs; Maya you'll prepare runbook; we (Summit) will send traces and success criteria. target timeline next week.
[08:58] Jordan Price: yes. i'll also include a short example benchmark from a similar customer in finance for reference (anonymized). any final questions?
[09:05] Priya Nair: one more do you support bring-your-own-model in private? we might want to host a fine-tuned model ourselves.

[09:11] Maya Chen: yes BYOM is supported in private and dedicated in some cases; we validate compatibility and provide onboarding steps. there are also licensing considerations for certain base models.
[09:21] Tom Delgado: thanks everyone. do you want to set the bench date now?
[09:24] Maya Chen: how about Wednesday 2026-03-11 10am PT? we can reserve 2 hours. jordan i'll add to calendar after pricing doc goes out.
[09:31] Priya Nair: that works for us. Alicia?
[09:33] Alicia Romero: yes works. thanks Jordan and team.
[09:36] Jordan Price: great, we'll follow up with the package. end of call.
[09:40] (meeting ends)
